newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Europe goes full steam ahead toward EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Europe goes full steam ahead toward EMU.

text.p: European financial leaders, rallied by German chancellor Helmut Kohl, have made clear Europe is moving into monetary union with an unstoppable momentum - the only question now is which countries will make the grade.
Kohl, widely seen as the main driving force behind European integration, said on Friday Europe's goal had to be to get a large number of fully-qualified nations into the union in 1999.
In a speech to the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt, Kohl said, "The goal must be that many nations meet the stability criteria and participate in the currency union from the beginning."

Finance ministers addressing the gathering of some 800 bankers reaffirmed their commitment to creating a stable European currency on time in 1999 and said they were determined their countries would be in at the start.
Most expect Europe's two financial power houses, France and Germany, to form a core group around which several smaller nations will form the first club of monetary union.
But Italy, not wanting to be left out, tried to keep its hopes alive, stressing progress already under way.
Antonio Fazio, Governor of the Bank of Italy, said the Rome government had asked for the Italian lira to be readmitted to Europe's exchange rate mechanism.
Responding to a question at the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt, Fazio said, "Our government has asked for the lira to re-enter the ERM."
The lira was forced out of the close-knit exchange rate system in 1992.

Spain's Economy Minister, Rodrigo de Rato, also keen to be in EMU at the start, said, "I believe by now there ought not to be many doubts...in financial markets that Spain finds itself on the right track to convergence and monetary union".

European countries which want to meld their currencies in the planned Euro from 1999 are scrambling to meet economic targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, budget deficits and public debt in the 1997 year.

Most European countries are facing the greatest problems in meeting the fiscal targets, which call for budget deficits to run at a maximum of three percent of gross domestic product and public debt at a maximum of 60 percent of GDP.
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis brushed aside worries that France's bid to cut its budget deficits to meet the Maastricht goal in 1997 was only a one-off effort.
"This effort is part of a strategy to cut the public deficit on a durable basis," he said.
Arthuis stressed that France intended to achieve long-term fiscal stability, adding that such discipline will be essential for the stability of the future European currency.
The French budget deficit would be within the three percent limit in 1997. France then intended to cut the deficit to 2.8 percent in 1998 and to below two percent by the year 2001.
Central bank officials, meanwhile, moved beyond the initial stage of monetary union, debating how nations unable to join the Euro in 1999 will eventually be brought into the fold.

Acknowledging that it was highly unlikely that all 15 European nations could join European Economic and Monetary Union at its launch in 1999, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer urged non-participants to join a so-called EMS II system at that time.
This system is intended to bind currencies which do not make the grade for EMU to the new Euro-currency.

"EMS II can generate a very important signal," Tietmeyer said, adding "What the signal must be is: all countries - whether they are already participants in monetry union or not -- want to strengthen convergence."
